A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same visual-token information and pruning study despite the changed title. All 13 pages of v1 and 14 pages of v2, including equations, figures, tables, and appendices, support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original pruning experiments, token-information analyses, benchmark results, and efficiency measurements for LLaVA-1.5-7B and Qwen2.5-VL-7B.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds alternative-metric experiments, an attention-versus-information case study, and InternVL3.5-8B results.

M1.justification: Appendix 12 introduces diagnostic scoring variants: marginal contribution removes a token from the full visual set, while sequence-level scoring averages ground-truth token probabilities across the answer. These change scoring procedures in the added tests; the original first-token score, Equations 1–6, and hybrid random-pruning procedures remain unchanged.

E1.justification: The additions reuse existing tasks and datasets. InternVL3.5-8B is tested on the same six benchmarks used in Section 4.2; adding this model changes experimental configuration, not dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Figures 13–14 add evaluated marginal-contribution and sequence-level alternatives against the original information metric. Comparator membership in the existing pruning benchmarks and Tables 1–3 is unchanged.

E3.justification: New experiments compare scoring variants with 72, 144, 288, and 432 retained tokens, using layer 3 on MME and layers 3 and 10 on TextVQA. Appendix 14 adds layer-wise evaluation of InternVL3.5-8B. Existing protocols and pruning settings in Tables 4–5 are retained; corrected MME axis labels do not establish a metric change.

E4.justification: New Appendices 12–14 substantially expand validation: they test sensitivity to singleton versus marginal contribution and first-token versus sequence-level scoring, examine attention distraction through a giraffe heatmap example, and test architectural generalization on InternVL3.5-8B. These address previously untested aspects of metric validity and mechanism.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing token-information distribution analysis is retained, and the additions introduce no new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: Original benchmark and efficiency results remain unchanged, but Figures 13–16 add substantial diagnostic results. Figure 13 reports standalone versus marginal MME scores of 2304 versus 2176 at 72 tokens, but 2207 versus 2258 at 432 tokens. Further additions show first-token scoring outperforming sequence-level scoring, persistence of the sequence-level horizon, an attention-information mismatch, and task-dependent horizon curves for InternVL3.5-8B.

T1.justification: Appendix 12 adds mathematical definitions in prose for marginal-contribution and sequence-level information, changing the reference token set and probability aggregation respectively. The original formal definitions and Equations 1–6 are unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution statements, and conclusion retain the same scientific claims: information vanishes with depth, horizon position depends on task and model, and random pruning complements existing methods. The retitling and added supporting experiments do not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: The new appendices attribute marginal scoring weaknesses to visual redundancy, sequence scoring weaknesses to error propagation, and harmful tokens to attention distraction. They also interpret the additional results as evidence of metric and architectural generality. These extend the earlier explanations, although Figure 13 contradicts the new claim that standalone scoring consistently matches or exceeds marginal scoring.

D1.justification: The abstract changes code availability from a future promise to a statement that code is available at the same repository. This is a reported access-status change; the PDFs retain the existing implementation, hardware, and pruning-setting disclosures.

R1.justification: v2 adds the InternVL3.5 reference to support the new architecture experiment. Existing related-work discussions and positioning against VTW, PDrop, and other pruning methods remain substantively unchanged; subsequent citation renumbering is cosmetic.

P1.justification: The title, author order, contact presentation, acknowledgments, and an appendix cross-reference are edited, and three focused appendix sections are appended. The existing scientific narrative and section sequence remain largely verbatim rather than extensively rewritten or reorganized.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 13–16 for metric comparisons, sequence-level behavior, heatmaps, and InternVL results. Several existing MME plots replace 'Accuracy' with 'Total Score', and baseline legends are adjusted. Page spacing and flow change modestly, while existing figure designs and table structures are largely preserved.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, Appendices 12–14 provide useful direct checks of the information metric and additional architectural validation, strengthening empirical support without altering the main results. Corrected MME labels and reported code availability also help. The gains are limited by overinterpretation: Figure 13 shows standalone scoring losing at 432 tokens despite the claimed consistent superiority, and the heatmap illustrates attention distraction without establishing the asserted causal correction mechanism.
